docs.title: Diabetes Mellitus
docs.text: A metabolic disorder characterized by elevated blood glucose due to insufficient insulin or insulin resistance.

docs.title: Types
docs.text:
• Type 1: Autoimmune destruction of insulin-producing cells.
  • Type 2: Insulin resistance with relative insulin deficiency.
  • Gestational: Occurs during pregnancy.

docs.title: Nursing Assessment
docs.text:
• Blood glucose monitoring
  • Signs of hypo- and hyperglycemia
  • Foot inspection
  • HbA1c review

docs.title: Heart Failure
docs.text: A clinical syndrome where the heart cannot pump enough blood to meet the body's needs.

docs.title: Types
docs.text:
• Left-sided failure: Blood backs up into the lungs. Symptoms: dyspnea, crackles, orthopnea.
  • Right-sided failure: Blood backs up into the systemic circulation. Symptoms: edema, JVD, weight gain.

docs.title: Nursing Assessment
docs.text:
• Daily weight
  • Intake and output
  • Lung sounds
  • Edema
  • Fatigue and activity tolerance

docs.title: Anatomy & Physiology
docs.text: Foundational concepts of human structure and function relevant to nursing practice.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Anatomy is the study of structure. Physiology is the study of function. Together they form the basis for understanding how the body works, how disease disrupts it, and how nursing interventions restore balance.

docs.title: Key Systems
docs.text: System Primary Function Nursing Relevance Cardiovascular Circulates blood, delivers oxygen BP, pulse, perfusion, edema Respiratory Gas exchange Rate, depth, oxygen saturation Nervous Coordinates body activities Consciousness, pain, reflexes Renal Filters blood, balances fluids Urine output, electrolytes Endocrine Hormonal regulation Blood glucose, thyroid, stress response

docs.title: Homeostasis
docs.text:
The body's tendency to maintain a stable internal environment. Most nursing care aims to support or restore homeostasis.

Core variables kept in balance: - Temperature - pH - Blood glucose - Fluid and electrolyte levels - Blood pressure

docs.title: Clinical Application
docs.text: When you assess a patient, you are checking how well their systems are maintaining homeostasis. Abnormal vitals are signals that one or more systems are under strain.

docs.title: Microbiology
docs.text: Microorganisms, infection, and the principles of asepsis in nursing practice.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Microbiology explains how pathogens cause disease and how the body defends against them. For nurses, it underpins infection control, antibiotic stewardship, and patient education.

docs.title: Key Concepts
docs.text:
• Pathogen: A microorganism that causes disease.
  • Commensal: A microorganism that lives on or in the body without causing harm.
  • Asepsis: Practices that prevent contamination by pathogens.
  • Sterile technique: Eliminating all microorganisms.
  • Clean technique: Reducing the number of microorganisms.

docs.title: Common Pathogen Classes
docs.text: Class Examples Notes Bacteria S. aureus, E. coli Treatable with antibiotics Viruses Influenza, HIV Require antivirals or vaccines Fungi Candida Often opportunistic Parasites Plasmodium Common in tropical regions

docs.title: Infection Control Basics
docs.text:
• Hand hygiene is the single most effective measure.
  • Use personal protective equipment appropriately.
  • Follow isolation precautions based on transmission route.
  • Dispose of sharps safely.

docs.title: Pharmacology Basics
docs.text: Core principles of how drugs work and how nurses safely administer them.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Pharmacology is the study of drugs and their effects on the body. Nurses need to understand pharmacokinetics, pharmacodynamics, and the nursing responsibilities that come with every dose.

docs.title: Key Terms
docs.text:
• Pharmacokinetics: What the body does to the drug (absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion).
  • Pharmacodynamics: What the drug does to the body.
  • Half-life: Time for the drug concentration to halve.
  • Therapeutic index: Margin between effective and toxic doses.
  • Side effect: Predictable, often unavoidable effect.
  • Adverse reaction: Harmful, sometimes unpredictable effect.

docs.title: The Rights of Medication Administration
docs.text:
1. Right patient
  2. Right drug
  3. Right dose
  4. Right route
  5. Right time
  6. Right documentation
  7. Right reason
  8. Right to refuse

docs.title: Nursing Responsibilities
docs.text:
• Verify the order.
  • Check allergies.
  • Know the drug's action and side effects.
  • Monitor the patient's response.
  • Educate the patient.
